Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ 2{x}^{2} & =3x \\ 2{x}^{2}-3x & =0 \\ x(2x-3) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation: 

- Substituting $x=0$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}) & \overset{?}{=}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2(0)^{2}) & \overset{?}{=}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3(0)) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0) & \overset{?}{=}\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

which is not valid because $\ln \left(0\right)$ is undefined. Therefore, $x=0$ is not a valid solution.

- Substituting $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}) & \overset{?}{=}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}) & \overset{?}{=}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3(\frac{3}{2})) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{2}).\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the only solution is $x =\dfrac{3}{2}.$
